That clarification does not change the counterexample or the zero-reserve theorem.1. Section 2 legitimately removes  $N=1$ The decisive distinction is between deriving zero reserve from a failure and using zero reserve to obtain local geometry. The preceding single-positive consequence used  $N=1$  for the former. The new theorem assumes  $R=0$ , so it needs only the latter.Let  $I$  index the original positive source occurrences in the complete fusion, and fix any  $i\in I$  with two actual marked sides. =A+U_0+Z_0+L_1+2L_{2\mathrm{bar}}
 +2L_{2\mathrm{mutual}}+L_3.$$
Every summand is nonnegative, so every listed count vanishes. Under the accepted physical interpretations, this gives:no activated positive terminals;no blank marked gates;fullness of every original  $2P0T$  tile, together with the other stated saturation consequences.Thus the chosen positive has two occupied marked gates and two unactivated positive terminals. This holds for every doubly marked positive in the same fusion. It does not require there to be only one positive.The preceding geometry, §§2–5, then applies inside the entire original fusion. No deletion of other positives or passage to a smaller fusion is needed. In particular:The support exclusion beside an unactivated terminal excludes original occupancy from every source. Its proof uses the retained selection, its already occupied anchor, and retention of original occupancy.The strict longitudinal clearance uses globally forced fullness of an original pair tile.The transverse-overlap argument uses disjointness of original endpoint sets.The common-owner classification separately handles both gates belonging to one original source.None of these steps counts positive sources or requires separation of final endpoint components. The source-role catalogue and rotor barrier enter with their supplied accepted local scope; the new proof does not obtain that scope merely by relabelling other positive sources as negative.Consequently, the new use of the preceding geometry is legitimate. It is an application of its local hypotheses under global saturation, rather than an extrapolation from the preceding  $N=1$  conclusion.2. Width six includes arbitrary independent unequal heights at  $R=0$ Suppose the chosen doubly marked positive has normalized dimensions
$$U(6,a,b),
\qquad a,b\ge4$$
with the permitted even heights.Choose a side of height  $\min(a,b)$ . Because the source is doubly marked, this shorter or equal side is marked. Because reserve is zero, its gate is occupied and its positive terminal is unactivated.The accepted width-six occupied-gate theorem says that an occupied marked gate on this shorter or equal side activates the corresponding positive terminal. This contradicts  $A=0$ .Therefore
$$R=0,\quad w=6
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{the positive source is not doubly marked}.$$
The argument uses neither  $a=b$  nor any upper bound on either height. It also does not require distinct owners for the two gates: one occupied marked gate on a shorter or equal side already gives the contradiction.This justifies the factor  $w\ne6$  in the exceptional predicate. In particular, a width-six positive with a very tall leg is still nonexceptional for this note. The conclusion needed here is the exclusion of double marking; the argument need not exclude every possible single mark on a longer side.3. The remaining dimension classification proves exactly the stated exceptionAfter excluding  $w=6$ , there are two cases.If  $w>10$ , the permitted even width satisfies  $w\ge12$ , so the source is exceptional immediately.If  $w\le10$ , apply the two-gate classification to the chosen source.Common owner. The preceding geometry, §5, gives one of the two complete nested-U forms. For the upright form,
$$4\le h\le a-4,\qquad 4\le k\le b-4,$$
and for the inverted form,
$$4\le h\le\min(a,b)-4.$$
Either way,
$$a\ge8,\qquad b\ge8.$$
Distinct owners. If both owners were transverse, their original endpoint footprints would contain, respectively,
$$\{(2,c):2\le c\le6\},
\qquad
\{(2,c):w-5\le c\le w-1\}.$$
For  $6\le w\le10$ , these footprints share  $(2,5)$ . Distinct original owners cannot share an endpoint. Hence at least one owner is longitudinal. Its accepted strict clearance gives
$$4\le h\le a-4
\quad\text{or}\quad
4\le h\le b-4,$$
so the corresponding positive height is at least eight.These cases establish, for every chosen doubly marked positive,
$$w\ne6
\quad\text{and}\quad
\bigl(w\ge12\ \text{or}\ \max(a,b)\ge8\bigr).$$
That is precisely the exceptional predicate in equation (4).The distinction between common and distinct ownership is essential, and the new proof preserves it correctly. It does not apply the distinct-owner overlap prohibition to a shared owner.4. The count  $n_2\le L$  uses no defect twiceDefine subsets of the original positive source indices:
$$I_2=\{i\in I:\text{both sides of }i\text{ are marked}\},$$

$$I_{\mathrm{exc}}=\{i\in I:\text{source }i\text{ is exceptional}\}.$$
The physical argument above proves
$$I_2\subseteq I_{\mathrm{exc}}.$$
The counting map is simply
$$i\longmapsto i.$$
It is injective, so
$$n_2=|I_2|\le |I_{\mathrm{exc}}|=L.$$
This is a count of original positive source occurrences. Equal dimension triples do not identify two distinct sources.Crucially, the map does not send positive sources to gate owners, pair tiles, activated terminals, or any other defect occurrence. If several local arguments involve a shared owner or other shared physical structure, each still establishes a necessary dimension property of its own chosen positive. Applying a universal zero-reserve consequence several times does not consume it.Thus the asserted injection has no hidden resource-reuse assumption. It is categorically different from the allocation that would be needed at  $R>0$ .5. The ledger identities and the zero-reserve theorem are correctWrite the sufficient ledger margin as
$$m=N+R-G.$$
The source census gives
$$\begin{aligned}
m
&=(n_0+n_1+n_2)+R-(n_1+2n_2)\\
&=n_0+R-n_2.
\end{aligned}$$
Using  $D=2R$ ,
$$m\ge0
\iff n_2\le n_0+R
\iff 2n_2\le2n_0+D.$$
Since these quantities are integral,
$$m<0
\iff n_2\ge n_0+R+1.$$
These are exact equivalences for nonnegativity or failure of the sufficient ledger margin. They are not equivalences for negativity of actual  $\sigma$ , because the supplied relation is only
$$\sigma\ge m.$$
There is also no second credit hidden in  $n_0$ . A positive source with  $g_i\in\{0,1,2\}$  marked sides contributes  $1-g_i$  to  $N-G$ :Marked sides  $g_i$ Contribution to  $N-G$ 0 $+1$ 1 $0$ 2 $-1$ The unmarked-source margin is already part of the original census.At zero reserve,
$$\sigma\ge m=n_0-n_2\ge n_0-L.$$
Therefore  $L\le n_0$  proves the sufficient joint allocation.For the displayed dimension class: $w=6$  makes the first conjunct of the exceptional predicate false, regardless of either height; $w\in\{8,10\}$  with  $a,b\in\{4,6\}$  makes both alternatives in its second conjunct false.Hence  $L=0$ , and in fact
$$n_2=0,\qquad \sigma\ge n_0\ge0.$$
This permits any finite number of positive sources. No step imposes a bound on that number.Likewise, a zero-reserve failure of the sufficient allocation requires
$$n_2\ge n_0+1,$$
and hence at least  $n_0+1$  distinct exceptional positive sources. This is a necessary obstruction count. It establishes no realizability in the exceptional range.6. The shared-defect target and parity counterexample have the correct scopeThe exact remaining budget target is
$$\boxed{\,2(n_2-n_0)\le D\,},$$
equivalently
$$2n_2\le D+2n_0.$$
Thus the proposed assignment has the correct units: two unit slots per doubly marked positive, a total of  $D$  weighted defect slots, and at most two additional slots per unmarked positive.Those two unmarked-source slots represent its existing one unit of ledger margin after multiplying the entire inequality by two. They do not create two units of reserve.An assignment that respects these capacities would prove the displayed inequality. A weight-two defect occurrence may supply two distinct slots, while a weight-one occurrence may supply only one. As the manuscript states, occurrence labels help specify nonreuse; they do not establish geometric availability. The accepted exact identity supplies the simultaneous aggregate accounting, and a further argument must establish whatever assignment or global inequality is claimed.The arithmetic example is correct:
$$n_0=n_1=0,\quad n_2=2,\quad
N=2,\quad G=4,\quad D=2,\quad R=1.$$
It satisfies  $D=2R$ , but
$$m=N+R-G=2+1-4=-1.$$
Two different unit defects can have assigned subtotals
$$d_1=d_2=1.$$
Separate rounding then produces
$$\left\lceil\frac{d_1}{2}\right\rceil+
\left\lceil\frac{d_2}{2}\right\rceil
=2,$$
although the reserve is only one.This disproves the inference
$$\text{one distinct unit defect per double mark}
+\text{global evenness}
\ \Longrightarrow\
\text{enough reserve to pay every double mark}.$$
It does not construct a physical fusion satisfying those counts. Nor does  $m=-1$  determine actual  $\sigma$ . The manuscript correctly preserves both limitations.The small clarification needed in the general paragraph is the exhaustion condition. The identity
$$\sum_j\left\lceil\frac{d_j}{2}\right\rceil
=\frac{\sum_jd_j+o}{2}$$
is correct for integer defect subtotals, where  $o$  counts the odd subtotals. To compare this with actual global reserve as an excess of  $o/2$ , explicitly require
$$\sum_jd_j=D.$$
A precise replacement sentence is:When the assigned subtotals partition the whole defect budget, so that  $\sum_j d_j=D$ , separate rounding exceeds the actual global reserve by  $o/2$ .If some defect capacity remains unassigned, write
$$E=D-\sum_jd_j\ge0.$$
Then the exact comparison is
$$\sum_j\left\lceil\frac{d_j}{2}\right\rceil-R
=\frac{o-E}{2}.$$
Disjoint assigned occurrences alone imply only  $\sum_jd_j\le D$ ; unused capacity can cover some or all of the rounding surcharge. The two-source example has  $E=0$ , so this clarification leaves its force unchanged.7.
